subject: chem
title: Organic Chemistry Basics
subtitle: Nomenclature, isomerism, reaction types and reagents.
concept: Organic molecules are named systematically using IUPAC rules based on longest carbon chain, functional groups, and substituents.
Structural isomers have the same molecular formula but different structural arrangements; stereoisomers have the same connectivity but different spatial arrangements.
Key reaction types: substitution, addition, elimination, hydrolysis, oxidation, reduction.

notes.heading: IUPAC Nomenclature
items: Identify the longest continuous carbon chain as the parent hydrocarbon (meth-, eth-, prop-, but-, pent-, hex-). Number the chain from the end that gives substituents/functional groups the lowest locants.

The principal functional group determines the suffix (parent name): –ane (alkane), –ene (alkene), –ol (alcohol), –al (aldehyde), –one (ketone), –oic acid (carboxylic acid). Substituents (methyl, bromo, chloro etc.) are listed alphabetically as prefixes with their position number.

notes.heading: Structural Isomers
items: Structural isomers have the same molecular formula but different structural arrangements. Three types: chain isomers (different carbon skeleton), positional isomers (same functional group at different positions on the chain), and functional group isomers (different functional group — e.g. an aldehyde and a ketone with the same formula).

notes.heading: Stereoisomers
items: E/Z isomerism (a type of geometric isomerism) arises when a C=C bond has two different groups on each carbon. The C=C bond has restricted rotation; Z (zusammen) isomers have the higher-priority groups on the same side; E (entgegen) have them on opposite sides. Priorities follow Cahn–Ingold–Prelog rules (higher atomic number = higher priority).

Optical isomers (enantiomers) arise when a molecule has a chiral centre — a carbon with four different groups. The two enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images with identical physical and chemical properties, except they rotate plane-polarised light by equal amounts in opposite directions. A 50:50 mixture (racemate) shows no net optical rotation.

notes.heading: Reaction Types and Mechanisms
items: Substitution: a group is replaced by another. Electrophilic substitution (benzene + Br₂ / FeBr₃), free-radical substitution (alkane + Cl₂ / UV), nucleophilic substitution (halogenoalkane + NaOH).
Addition: two molecules join across a π bond. Electrophilic addition (alkene + Br₂), hydrogenation (alkene + H₂).
Elimination: a small molecule is lost from within a molecule to create a π bond (e.g. alcohol → alkene by dehydration). Hydrolysis: a bond is broken using water (e.g. ester hydrolysis).

An electrophile is an electron-deficient species that accepts electron pairs. A nucleophile is electron-rich (lone pair or negative charge) and donates electron pairs. Curly arrows show movement of electron pairs — always from electrons to electron-deficient site.

definitions.body: A carbon atom bonded to four different groups, giving rise to non-superimposable mirror image molecules (enantiomers).
A type of stereoisomerism about a C=C double bond, where restricted rotation and different groups on each carbon give rise to E (opposite sides) and Z (same side) isomers.
An electron-deficient species that accepts a lone pair of electrons from a nucleophile; attacks regions of high electron density.
An electron-rich species (lone pair or negative charge) that donates electrons to an electron-deficient atom.

steps.text: Cl on C2 (number from end nearest substituent)

workedExamples.q: Explain why but-2-ene shows E/Z isomerism but but-1-ene does not.

steps.text: CH₃CH=CHCH₃: C2 has CH₃ and H; C3 has CH₃ and H → two different groups on each carbon of C=C → E/Z isomerism exists.
CH₂=CHCH₂CH₃: C1 has two H atoms → both groups on C1 are identical → no E/Z isomerism.

mistakes: Numbering the chain from the wrong end — always number to give the lowest locants to substituents/functional groups.
Forgetting that E/Z isomerism requires TWO DIFFERENT groups on EACH doubly-bonded carbon.
Confusing optical isomers with E/Z isomers — optical isomers require a chiral centre (4 different groups on one sp3 C).
tips: For naming: write out the full structural formula first, then identify the longest chain.
Enantiomers have identical physical and chemical properties except: they rotate plane-polarised light in opposite directions and react differently with other chiral molecules.
Learn the test for each functional group: carboxylic acid (Na₂CO₃ — CO₂ effervescence), aldehyde (Tollens' — silver mirror; Fehling's — brick red ppt), alkene (bromine water — decolourised).

flashcards.a: A carbon atom bonded to four different groups — produces non-superimposable mirror image molecules (enantiomers).

flashcards.q: What is the difference between E and Z isomers?
flashcards.a: E (entgegen): higher priority groups on opposite sides of C=C. Z (zusammen): higher priority groups on the same side.

flashcards.q: What are the two conditions for E/Z isomerism?
flashcards.a: (1) Restricted rotation (usually a C=C bond). (2) Two different groups on each of the doubly-bonded carbons.
An electron-rich species (lone pair or negative charge) that donates a pair of electrons to an electron-deficient atom.

flashcards.q: What reaction type occurs when an alcohol loses water to form an alkene?

flashcards.a: They are non-superimposable mirror images; they rotate plane-polarised light by equal amounts in opposite directions; identical in all other physical/chemical properties.

questions.q: What is the IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CH₃?
questions.exp: Longest chain = 4C (butane); OH on C2 (numbered from end nearest OH) → butan-2-ol.

questions.q: Which of these has a chiral centre?
questions.exp: CH₃CH(Cl)CH₂CH₃: the C bearing Cl has 4 different groups (H, Cl, CH₃, CH₂CH₃) → chiral centre.

questions.q: But-2-ene can exist as E and Z isomers. What condition makes this possible?
opts: C=C has restricted rotation and different groups on each carbon
It has more than one functional group
questions.exp: E/Z isomerism requires restricted rotation (C=C) and two different groups on each carbon of the double bond.

questions.q: Which reaction type best describes: CH₂=CH₂ + Br₂ → CH₂BrCH₂Br?
questions.exp: Two molecules (ethene and Br₂) join across the double bond — electrophilic addition.

questions.q: What is the relationship between enantiomers?
opts: They rotate plane-polarised light in the same direction
questions.exp: Enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images — they rotate plane-polarised light by equal amounts in opposite directions.

recall: Apply IUPAC rules to name branched-chain alkanes and compounds with functional groups.
Distinguish between structural isomers and stereoisomers.
Explain the conditions required for E/Z isomerism.
Explain what a chiral centre is and give an example.
